text.en: Asha used a map to find her way. "What do these symbols mean?" she asked.

A map is a selective view of an area, often shown from above. Mapmakers use a scale and symbols to show certain features clearly. Its parts include the title, scale, direction, legend and symbols. The scale shows how distances on the map relate to the ground, and the four main directions are north, south, east and west.
Parallels of latitude extend east–west. Meridians of longitude join the poles. Latitude measures north or south of the Equator, and longitude measures east or west of the Prime Meridian. The Equator is 0 degrees latitude and the Prime Meridian is 0 degrees longitude. Longitude helps explain differences in local solar time. Actual time-zone boundaries can follow political and administrative choices.
Maps show relief with contour lines, and we use colours and symbols for features. Topographic maps and the Survey of India sheets help us study areas. GIS and satellite images are modern aids.

text.en: A map cannot show every object or detail. Decide what question the map answers, then look at its title. A road map and a rainfall map select different information.

board.text: Match the map to the question

text.en: A physical map emphasises landforms or water features. A political map may emphasise boundaries and settlements. A thematic map displays a subject such as population or rainfall.

board.text: Physical · political · thematic

text.en: A map legend explains what particular symbols and colours represent. Use the legend for that map. A colour can represent different things on two maps.

board.text: Read the legend before interpreting a symbol

text.en: The map’s north arrow gives orientation. East lies to the right when north points upward. A rotated map can still show the same directions.

board.text: Use the north mark, not just the page edge

text.en: A word scale can say one centimetre represents five hundred metres. Measure two and a half centimetres at that scale to get one thousand two hundred fifty metres.
A representative fraction uses the same units on both sides. One to fifty thousand says one centimetre on the map represents fifty thousand centimetres on the ground.

board.text: 1 : 50,000 → 1 cm represents 500 m

text.en: A graphic scale draws units as marks on a bar. If a digital image is resized uniformly, the bar resizes with the map and can still be used for comparison.

board.text: A graphic bar scales with the graphic

text.en: A larger-scale map shows a smaller area with more possible detail. One to ten thousand is a larger scale than one to one million because its fraction is greater.

board.text: Larger scale has a smaller denominator

text.en: Straight-line distance and route distance can differ. For a path with turns, measure each section or use a flexible line to follow the route before applying the scale.

board.text: Choose straight-line or route distance

text.en: Ordinary compass directions describe one place relative to another. Coordinates can identify a position directly. A pair of geographic coordinates needs both latitude and longitude.

board.text: Direction and position answer different questions

text.en: Read a geographic location as latitude first, then longitude in the convention used here. For ten north and eighty east, move north of the Equator and east of the Prime Meridian.
Meridians meet at the poles, while parallels do not. The east–west distance represented by one degree of longitude becomes smaller toward the poles.

board.text: Longitude lines converge toward the poles

text.en: A contour joins points at equal elevation. The contour interval tells you how much elevation changes between adjacent contour lines.

board.text: Read the contour interval from the legend

text.en: At the same map scale and contour interval, closely spaced contours indicate a steeper slope. More widely spaced contours show a gentler slope.

board.text: Closely spaced contours → steeper slope

text.en: Several closed contour lines can mark a hill if the labelled elevations increase inward. Check the numbers before deciding whether the centre is higher or lower.

board.text: Check whether elevations rise or fall inward

text.en: Topographic sheets use symbols and lines to show relief, drainage, roads and settlements. The size of a symbol may be chosen for legibility rather than to measure the real object.

board.text: Read topographic features together

text.en: Remote sensing obtains information without touching the area being observed. An aircraft or satellite may carry a sensor that records energy from land or water.

board.text: Remote sensing uses observations from a distance

text.en: An aerial photo and a satellite image can show different extents and levels of detail. A mapmaker checks the date, coverage and resolution before comparing them.

board.text: Image date, coverage and resolution matter

text.en: A geographic information system can combine layers for roads, rivers, land use and other data. Each layer needs suitable location information and should be checked for accuracy.

board.text: GIS lets us compare layers on a common map

text.en: A navigation receiver uses signals from several satellites to estimate position. GPS is one satellite navigation system, and GNSS is the wider term for such systems.

board.text: GNSS estimates a position from signals

text.en: The chapter introduces Bhuvan as an example of an Indian geospatial platform. Depending on the layer, a geospatial viewer can help explore imagery and mapped features together.

board.text: Geospatial viewers can combine mapped information

text.en: Before trusting a map answer, check its title, date, direction, scale and legend. Then describe how you read the answer so someone else can repeat the steps.

board.text: Check context, read the map and show your method

problem.en: Two points are 2.5 cm apart on a map at 1 : 50,000. What is the straight-line ground distance?

text.en: Multiply two point five centimetres by fifty thousand.

why.en: This gives one hundred twenty-five thousand centimetres on the ground.

text.en: Divide by one hundred to convert centimetres to metres.

why.en: The straight-line distance is one thousand two hundred fifty metres.

prompt.en: A friend says The Equator is 0 degrees longitude. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: The Prime Meridian is 0 degrees longitude.
